Where your AI cost estimate goes wrong

Cost-Route prices an AI workload across three procurement routes on live catalogue data, gates the candidates on a quality bar before it looks at price, and shows where a buyer's own estimate went wrong. Two worked examples are measured end to end; the panel just below prices your own numbers at those measured rates.

Prices read from OpenRouter and the Hugging Face router at 2026-09-15T16:39:21.051Z. Page generated 2026-09-21T08:51:27.630Z.

How to read this page

  1. Pick a workload. Use the tabs: Legal contract review or Image generation.
  2. Read the gap. Each tab opens with three numbers: what the buyer said the month would cost, what their own stated assumptions cost when priced out, and what the calls actually cost. The first gap is arithmetic; the second is the measurement.
  3. Move your own numbers. Volume, prompt size, answer length and your own estimate are yours to change in the panel just below. Every measured figure stays locked and timestamped.
measured produced by a real, billed call at a timestamp. It does not move. assumed the buyer's input, or yours. Move it and the answer travels. PASS FAIL whether a candidate cleared the quality bar; not measured means no usable run.

Mechanics this route never exercised

Absent rather than zero. A row reading $0.00 beside a mechanic that never ran looks like a saving nobody took; these are mechanics that were never available here.

The same measurement, cut by question kind

One accuracy figure per candidate hides which questions the candidates separate on. This is the same run, re-cut: how many of each kind of question each candidate answered correctly, over the calls that were served. A question that was never answered is named under the cell rather than counted as a wrong answer.

CandidateStated in one clauseNeeds two clauses combinedNot answered by the contract

1 fabricated

OpenAI: GPT-5 Mini10/103/31/1

No candidate answered a Stated in one clause, Not answered by the contract question wrongly. Every difference the quality bar actually found is in “Needs two clauses combined”, and it is what fails GPT-4o-mini. A workload made only of the first kind has no measured reason to prefer the more expensive candidate. A low score on a kind is a failure to weigh against that candidate's price; a perfect score on a kind everyone passes is not a reason to buy it.

The three procurement routes

Route C is an estimate built from named assumptions, not a quoted price, and it is the only row in the repository with no monthly cost field. Sorting it beside A and B as though it were one more price is the mistake this table exists to prevent.

  • Licence is named and readable: "gemma". With a closed model the equivalent terms are in a vendor agreement, not a file you can inspect.
  • 2 providers list this model and 2 are live, so a failing provider can be swapped for another without changing the model. Note that only 1 of the 2 live providers publishes a price, so the fallback route cannot be costed from the catalogue.
  • No cache pricing is published on this route, so the prompt-caching discount that dominates the measured cost on route A does not apply here.
  • Gated: the Hub reports gated: "manual", so access requires an accepted licence before any call can be made. That is a real step, and it is not in the price.
  • The licence is a bespoke or restricted one ("gemma"), not Apache or MIT. It carries use restrictions that a permissive licence does not, and they are the buyer's to check.

Assumptions this page rests on

  • Synthetic documents. The contract and every question are invented for this benchmark, with known correct answers. No client documents, no scraped contracts, no real counterparty names.
  • A 14-question golden set. Chosen to include deliberate hard cases rather than sampled at random. The quality bar is 75% correct and at most 0 fabricated answers.
  • A 15,000 ms latency ceiling, the buyer's own number. Latency is reported against that ceiling, not against a generic target.
  • The buyer's estimate is an input, not a finding. 20,000 requests a month, 1,500 prompt tokens and 50 answer tokens per request, $18.00/month were stated by the buyer, not measured. The page's argument is the distance between those inputs and the measurement.
  • Prices were read at a timestamp. Catalogue rates were read 2026-09-15T16:39:21.051Z, and the calls behind this tab were made 2026-09-17T10:18:55.206Z. Re-running the pipeline reproduces the method, not these figures.
  • Route C is an estimate. Self-hosting has no published price, so its row is built from named assumptions and is never compared numerically with the two quoted routes.

What this tab cannot tell you

  • One workload. These numbers describe answering one question from one contract. A different task has different token counts, a different cache hit rate, and probably a different winner.
  • A cache hit rate that was measured once. Moving the prompt size scales the cached and uncached halves together, holding the measured hit rate fixed. A prompt with a different shape caches differently.
  • Quality that does not travel. The gate result is for this model on these 14 questions. It is evidence, not a guarantee about your questions.
  • Prices that drift. Every rate here was read at 2026-09-15T16:39:21.051Z. Re-run the pipeline for today's.

The candidates, and what they drew

There is no quality gate on this workload, and that is a statement about the measurement rather than about the models. Image output has no correct-share to compute, so the only machine gate is the buyer's own 15,000ms latency ceiling. The pictures are shown so the judgement that the machine cannot make is one a reader can.

Latency and cost are summed over different sets of runs on purpose. A call that returned no picture took some amount of time that was not a generation time, so it is left out of the latency figures; it was billed for the tokens it burned getting there, so it is left in the cost. Two rules pointing opposite ways, and dropping the failed runs from the cost would understate the monthly figure this workload exists to produce.

The open-weight route on this workload, read rather than measured

Neither of these was called. The Hugging Face router catalogue carries 140 models and none of them declare an image output, and the BFL routes that would serve FLUX directly are behind an account with no credit balance - so there is no route to run and no published rate to quote. What is readable is the model card's licence field, and that is what this table reports.

A licence is the one thing on this page that costs nothing to read and cannot be measured. It is still a purchase decision: the permissive row and the restricted row are the same weights with different terms, and the terms decide whether the cheaper one is usable at all.

Assumptions this page rests on

  • One fixed prompt. a single red circle on a plain white background is the exact string that was sent and billed. It is the workload, not an example of one. There is no golden set and no machine quality gate here, because whether a picture is any good is a human judgement.
  • A 15,000 ms latency ceiling, the buyer's own number and the only machine gate on this workload. Latency is reported against that ceiling, not against a generic target.
  • The buyer's estimate is an input, not a finding. 2,000 requests a month, 30 prompt tokens and 1,000 answer tokens per request, $25.00/month were stated by the buyer, not measured. The page's argument is the distance between those inputs and the measurement.
  • Prices were read at a timestamp. Catalogue rates were read 2026-09-15T16:39:21.051Z, and the calls behind this tab were made 2026-09-17T10:20:29.941Z. Re-running the pipeline reproduces the method, not these figures.
  • Route C is an estimate. Self-hosting has no published price, so its row is built from named assumptions and is never compared numerically with the two quoted routes.

What this tab cannot tell you

  • Latency that came back unverified. Two runs is two runs. The pair above moved 70x between one day and the next on identical input, and nothing in the response says whether a provider cache was involved. Read the cost column as measured and the latency column as observed twice.
  • An image token count that is deterministic, and a bill that is not. The picture costs the same number of tokens every time; the prompt and reasoning tokens around it move run to run, so the total is a narrow band rather than a figure.
  • Quality that nobody measured. The pictures are shown so a reader can judge them. That is a different kind of evidence from the text tab's correct-share and it does not transfer to a different prompt, style or aspect ratio.
  • The open-weight route. FLUX is reported from its licence field, not called. No price on that row was measured, and the table says which column was read.
  • Prices that drift. Every rate here was read at 2026-09-15T16:39:21.051Z. Re-run the pipeline for today's.

Where this comes from, and how to run it on your own workload

This page is the artifact. The pipeline that produces it — the benchmark runner, the estimate-versus-measured ledger, the renderer, the saved run files and the test suite — is in the repository, together with the n8n workflow that orchestrates the calls. Point it at your own contract or prompt and your own shortlist by adding one workload file, and the same report comes back with your numbers in it.

  • Repository: github.com/therealmaddieli/cost-route — code, workload files, the n8n workflow, and a README with setup.
  • This page, linkable: therealmaddieli.github.io/cost-route
  • Built with: n8n for orchestration and raw HTTP requests, and Claude Code as the agentic coding tool. Every measured claim on this page is backed by a test or a saved run file.
